title: Adaptive page migration policy — simulation notes
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This doc collects notes and early results from a set of policy simulations exploring adaptive page-migration heuristics for the KV cache. Motivation: observed tail latency spikes in multi-tenant runs that correlate with cross-node page migrations and PCIe/NVLink bursts. Hypothesis: conservative, access-pattern-aware migration policies can improve reuse locality (fewer long-tail page faults and lower remote-bandwidth peaks) without causing harmful migration churn that amplifies paging IO.

High-level idea:
- Maintain lightweight per-page "hotness delta" (recent_access_rate - baseline) sampled at coarse granularity (100ms windows).
- Trigger migration from remote node -> local node when hotness delta exceeds a threshold AND estimated migration cost (bytes / current_remote_bw) is less than expected savings window (predicted future local hits * average token bytes).
- Backoff migration if recent migration success ratio < 50% or if remote bandwidth > 70% saturation.

Why different from previous work in this folder:
- Focus on adaptive decisions that incorporate an online estimate of cross-node BW and per-page predicted hit-window (probabilistic) rather than simpler TTL/pinning heuristics or fixed thresholds.
- Emphasis on simulation first (trace-driven) to tune parameters before kernel-level prototyping.

Traces used:
- prod-embeddings-2025q1.trace (sampled client traffic, anonymized token IDs). 48-hour sample, heavy embeddings + short chat generations (seqlen 64 avg).
- internal-search-2025q2.trace (mixed long-context completions, seqlen 1024 tail).
- synthetic-hotburst-1k.trace (artificial hotkey surges to stress migration/backpressure).
All traces preprocessed to page-aligned accesses (page_size=2MB and 64KB experiments).

Hardware baseline for simulation:
- 2-socket host, each socket attached to 2x A100-40GB GPU nodes (simulated), dual NVMe per node.
- Sim network model: NVLink 200 GB/s intra-socket, inter-socket PCIe/NVLink/IB modeled with a 40–100 GB/s dynamic window depending on background load.
- Memory bandwidth per GPU/host channel: 700 GB/s (peak), throttled by contending traffic in multi-tenant scenarios.

Policies simulated (short names):
1) baseline-no-migration: only local residency and eviction; remote pages fetched on fault (cold-path) but never migrated proactively.
2) eager-migrate: move hot pages immediately on detection of N accesses in 50ms window (N tuned).
3) ttl-pin: short-duration pin + TTL reset on access (existing heuristics we've used).
4) adaptive-migrate (this experiment): the policy described above with cost-benefit check.
5) adaptive-migrate-lite: same as 4 but without bandwidth-aware backoff (to isolate BW effect).

Metrics collected:
- local_hit_rate (fraction of accesses served by local residency)
- reuse_win_dist (distribution of time between repeated accesses to same page)
- migration_bytes_per_minute
- migration_success_ratio (migrations that actually reduced remote fetches in next 10s)
- remote_bw_tail (99th percentile of remote bandwidth usage in GB/s)
- p99 end-to-end latency for token generation (measured at request level)
- page_fault_rate and NVMe paging IO (GB/min)

Key results (summary):
- baseline-no-migration: local_hit_rate=52%. p99 latency=220ms. remote_bw_tail peaked at 60 GB/s during burst traces.
- eager-migrate: local_hit_rate=74% but migration_bytes_per_minute increased 6x; migration_success_ratio=48%. p99 latency slightly improved in steady state (190ms) but worsened during hotkey bursts due to migration storms (p99=330ms). NVMe IO up due to spillbacks.
- ttl-pin: local_hit_rate=68%, migration_bytes_per_minute moderate; p99=205ms. Performed ok on steady workloads but failed to adapt to sudden pattern shifts.
- adaptive-migrate-lite: local_hit_rate=72%, migration_bytes_per_minute=2.1x baseline, success_ratio=62%, p99=180ms, remote_bw_tail=48 GB/s. Better than eager but still produced oscillations when access patterns shifted quickly.
- adaptive-migrate (bandwidth-aware backoff ON): local_hit_rate=71%, migration_bytes_per_minute=1.6x baseline, success_ratio=78%, p99=165ms, remote_bw_tail=35 GB/s, NVMe paging decreased by ~18% vs ttl-pin.

Interpretation / interesting observations:
- Bandwidth-aware backoff is the single most important knob to prevent migration storms: policies that ignore current cross-node BW can flood links and cause higher p99s.
- The cost-benefit predictor (simple exponential moving average to project next-window hits) reduced wasted migrations; success ratio increased from ~50% to ~78%.
- Page-size matters: with 2MB pages migration bytes are coarse-grained; adaptive policy benefits more from smaller page sizes (64KB) where migration cost is lower but metadata overhead and CPU sampling cost increase. We saw biggest p99 gains with hybrid approach (migrate 64KB subpages inside 2MB superpages when hotness is concentrated).
- For synthetic hotburst traces, adaptive policy sometimes caches aggressively on the wrong host if traffic distribution shifts across GPUs every few seconds; adding a short randomized dampening (jitter windows) reduced flip-flopping.

Design notes / heuristics tuned in sim:
- hotness_delta_window: 100ms sample with EMA alpha=0.2
- migration_threshold: delta > 12 accesses in window for 64KB pages, scaled linearly with page size
- predicted_savings_window: 5s default (weights longer for embedding workloads)
- bw_backoff_threshold: do not migrate if estimated_remote_bw_util > 70% or if concurrent_migrations > 8 per node
- migration_hysteresis: once migrated, do not re-migrate same page for 3s unless cold-access pattern resumes

Open questions and risks:
- Sampling overhead at 64KB granularity increases CPU overhead on the runtime agent; need microbenchmarks to quantify. Does the extra CPU cost offset token savings? (ACTION: Evan to run agent CPU proxy microbench, ticket INF-6190)
- Interaction with KV eviction and reserve window: migrating many pages into a node can cause local evictions that kick out other hot pages; need coordinated eviction-aware migration (global scoring).
- Security/tenancy: migrating pages between tenants/isolated pools may violate policies — ensure migration is disabled for strict-isolation customers.
- Kernel/proto-level implementation complexity: ideally implement migration orchestration in userspace (runtime agent) with ND-range copy ops vs kernel page remap. Which is faster on our infra?

Next steps (prio order):
1) Short experiments in staging with reduced sampling (64KB hybrid) to measure agent CPU: Evan (INF-6190) — target week of 2025-12-08.
2) Implement simple bandwidth meter in runtime that exposes current remote_bw_util and concurrent_migration_count to decision logic — Tomas (PR draft linked in artifacts).
3) Re-run mixed-production traces with hybrid subpage migration and measure p99 across tenants. Goal: p99 < 170ms and NVMe IO reduction > 15% compared to ttl-pin.
4) Prototype coordinated migration + eviction scoring (sketch attached in confluence page) — Lina/Evan pair.

Notes for implementation prototype (sketch):
- Decision plane lives as a lightweight thread in agent process, accepts page access samples via ring buffer from main-serving thread.
- Migration performed via GPUDirect peer copy when possible, falling back to host-side scatter-gather for cross-socket transfers. Record timings for success_ratio calculation.
- Expose telemetry: migration_decisions, migration_bytes, predicted_win, decision_latency. Add tracing hooks to console rollouts for staged canary.

Questions for the group (please reply inline):
- Is 70% remote_bw_util an OK default backoff for our current staging infra? We might pick 60–80 depending on observed tail.
- Acceptable CPU overhead threshold for the agent (we have limited headroom on c5n-like hosts) — suggest 3–5% of CPU baseline for sampling.

Attachments / artifacts referenced (plots are in the confluence page):
- sim-plots/migration-success-by-policy.png (heatmap of success_ratio across traces)
- sim-plots/remote-bw-tail-comparison.png
- sim-logs/example-flipflop-trace-20251120.txt

TODO (quick checklist):
- [ ] Evan: agent microbench (INF-6190)
- [ ] Tomas: bandwidth meter PR review & perf tests
- [ ] Lina: prototype coordinated eviction scoring
- [ ] Priya: validate isolation policy integration for private deployments

If folks want to riff on the cost estimator model: current predictor is intentionally simple (EMA * linear prediction). We should consider a lightweight bayesian filter that can better estimate short-term windows but keep compute low.

— Lina
